items.abstract: <jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title><jats:p>In this paper, we investigate the distribution of zeros of the independence polynomial of hypergraphs of maximum degree . For graphs, the largest zero‐free disk around zero was described by Shearer as having radius . Recently, it was shown by Galvin et al. that for hypergraphs the disk of radius  is zero‐free; however, it was conjectured that the actual truth should be . We show that this is indeed the case. We also show that there exists an open region around the interval  that is zero‐free for hypergraphs of maximum degree , which extends the result of Peters and Regts from graphs to hypergraphs. Finally, we determine the radius of the largest zero‐free disk for the family of bounded degree ‐uniform linear hypertrees in terms of  and .</jats:p>
title: Optimal Zero‐Free Regions for the Independence Polynomial of Bounded Degree Hypergraphs

items.abstract: <jats:p>The goal of this paper is to accurately describe the maximal zero-free region of the independence polynomial for graphs of bounded degree, for large degree bounds. In the previous work with de Boer, Guerini, and Regts, it was demonstrated that this zero-free region coincides with the normality region of the related occupation ratios. These ratios form a discrete semigroup that is in a certain sense generated by finitely many rational maps. We will show that as the degree bound converges to infinity, the properly rescaled normality regions converge to a limit domain, which can be described as the maximal boundedness component of a semigroup generated by infinitely many exponential maps. We prove that away from the real axis this boundedness component avoids a neighborhood of the boundary of the limit cardioid, answering a recent question by Andreas Galanis. We also give an exact formula for the boundary of the boundedness component near the positive real boundary point.</jats:p>
title: The Limit of the Zero Locus of the Independence Polynomial for Bounded Degree Graphs

items.abstract:
<jats:p>The Lovelace Threshold is a conceptual diagnostic device that exposes where the assumptions of current governance frameworks no longer match the operational logic of generative and autonomous systems. It names the point at which a governance mechanism stops being reliable because it was designed for a world in which a governed system is fully legible, fully bounded, and fully predictable in advance. In such settings, rules can be written around visible governable bodies. That's the Lovelace World, where systems merely execute predefined instructions. But now systems have evolved, we can recombine, or generate downstream effects that exceed explicit specification, and visible governance becomes structurally insufficient. That's the Post-Lovelace World, where systems anticipate, generate, and act beyond explicit specification. The gap between the two is a structural vulnerability that operates beyond current political frameworks' reach. This short note argues that the threshold applies beyond AI to any governance regime that depends on incomplete visibility into the substrate it seeks to regulate. The remedy is not only better after-the-fact enforcement, but upstream controls grounded in provenance, transformation accountability, and verifiable attestation.

items.abstract: <jats:p>We present a deterministic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for the independence polynomial ZG(λ) of graphs with maximum degree ∆, operating in the recently established non-disk zero-free region R∆ containing the interval [0, λc(∆)), where λc(∆) = (∆-1) ∆-1 (∆-2) ∆ marks the algorithmic threshold for the Hard-Core model. Our algorithm achieves running time O n O(log ∆) • poly log 1 ϵ and constitutes the first approximation scheme that fully exploits the non-disk geometry of the zero-free region. We further extend our framework to the left half-plane Re(λ) ≤ 0 and provide a multivariate generalization. Our results establish that the equivalence between zero-freeness and efficient approximability, previously known only for disk-shaped regions, extends to general complex domains with appropriate geometric conditions. As a corollary, we obtain an improved constructive version of the Lovász Local Lemma with explicit dependence on the Shearer parameters.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>We establish a tight complexity boundary for Hamiltonian Cycle in bipar tite graphs with ordered neighborhoods: the problem is polynomial-time solvable for graphs where each vertex has at most two neighbor intervals, and becomes NP-complete when three intervals are allowed. Specifically, we present an O(n3) dynamic programming algorithm for detecting Hamilto nian cycles in bipartite graphs G = (X,Y,E) where each vertex in Y has neighbors forming at most two contiguous intervals in a given ordering of X (2-interval bipartite graphs). This establishes a tight boundary between tractability and intractability: when three intervals are allowed, the problem becomes NP-complete, as we demonstrate via a polynomial-time reduction from Hamiltonian Cycle in chordal bipartite graphs. Our algorithm exploits a key structural property—that any partial Hamiltonian path maintains at most two “open” vertices (vertices with one incident edge awaiting a second connection)— enabling a polynomial-sized state space. The complexity clas sification is complete for k ≤ 3 neighbor intervals: convex bipartite graphs (k = 1) are solvable in linear time, 2-interval graphs (k = 2) are solvable in O(n3) time, and 3-interval graphs (k = 3) are NP-complete.</jats:p>
title: Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Hamiltonian Cycle in Bipartite Graphs with Bounded Neighbor Intervals
